title: Susannah Thompson: Courtship, Marriage, and Family Life with Susannah Spurgeon
seoTitle: Susannah Thompson: Marriage & Family Life | Charles Spurgeon
description: Discover the profound love story, mutual suffering, and enduring partnership of Charles and Susannah Spurgeon, including the founding of her monumental Book Fund.

content.text: First Impressions and a Blossoming Romance

When the young, country-born Charles Haddon Spurgeon arrived in London to preach at the historic New Park Street Chapel, he drew the attention of the entire congregation—though not all initial impressions were entirely favorable. Among the congregants was a beautiful, refined young woman named Susannah Thompson. Born on January 15, 1832, Susannah initially felt very little romantic attraction toward the new pastor, finding his rural manners, unpolished attire, and rustic appearance somewhat off-putting.

However, as she sat under his powerful, gospel-saturated preaching, her spiritual life was profoundly awakened. The young preacher's earnestness and undeniable spiritual unction won not only her theological respect but ultimately her heart. Their spiritual and personal relationship deepened rapidly, and in 1855, Spurgeon had the joy of publicly baptizing her upon her profession of faith.

Their courtship culminated in marriage on January 8, 1856. The union between Charles and "Susie" (as she was affectionately known) was characterized by an exemplary and profound devotion that would weather extraordinary storms. Shortly after their wedding, on September 20, 1856, the couple welcomed their only children into the world: twin sons named Charles and Thomas.

The Spurgeon household was a sanctuary of deep piety and mutual support. Susannah was the anchor of Charles's demanding and often overwhelming public life. While he was preaching to thousands and managing dozens of charitable institutions, she cultivated a home environment of grace, theological richness, and unwavering love. Their devotion to one another is famously captured in the title of a modern biographical work detailing their love story: Yours, Till Heaven.

The Spurgeon marriage was far from an easy, untroubled Victorian romance; it was heavily refined in the crucible of physical and emotional suffering. In 1868, when she was in her mid-thirties, Susannah developed severe gynecological health issues. In 1869, she underwent surgery performed by the renowned Scottish physician Dr. James Young Simpson, but she spent much of the remainder of her life as a practical invalid, frequently confined to her home or bed.

Simultaneously, Charles suffered from agonizing physical ailments, most notably a severe and chronic form of gout, Bright's disease (a degenerative kidney condition), and frequent, debilitating bouts of dark depression. Because of Susannah's physical limitations, she was often too ill to even leave her home to hear her husband preach at the Metropolitan Tabernacle. Yet, instead of allowing illness to drive a wedge between them, their mutual suffering forged an unbreakable spiritual bond, characterized by deep empathy and shared reliance on the sovereign grace of God.
The Book Fund and a Lasting Legacy

Despite her physical invalidism, Susannah Spurgeon refused to remain idle in the work of the Kingdom. She proved to be an indispensable partner in her husband's ministry. Recognizing the extreme poverty of many rural pastors across England—men who faithfully preached the Gospel but could barely afford to feed their families, let alone purchase theological books—Susannah founded "Mrs. Spurgeon's Book Fund" in 1875.

Operating largely from her sickbed, she managed a vast charitable enterprise. By the time of her death on October 22, 1903, her Book Fund had distributed an astonishing 200,000 theological books to needy ministers, providing them with vital intellectual and spiritual nourishment.

Susannah was also a gifted writer and editor. She documented her remarkable charitable work in the book Ten Years of My Life in the Service of the Book Fund (1886). Most notably, after Charles's death in 1892, Susannah dedicated her remaining years to preserving his legacy, serving as the primary co-editor and contributor to his massive, four-volume Autobiography, ensuring that the story of God's grace in the life of the "Prince of Preachers" would be passed down to future generations.
